ORBIT DESIGN SYSTEM

The shared language for type, color, icon, and interaction.

Orbit is Deloitte's design system — the tokens, components, and documented patterns that keep every product surface consistent, accessible, and unmistakably on-brand, instead of each team rebuilding its own version of the same button.

456
design tokens
73
icons
25
components
2
themes, light & dark

Foundations

Colors & Tokens

Brand, neutral, and status palettes — mapped from primitive scale to semantic token, in both themes.

Typography

One typeface, Inter, across a 15-step scale from Display down to Label.

Spacing & radius

A 9-step spacing scale and a 7-step corner-radius scale shared by every component.

Iconography

73 glyphs bound to icon-* color tokens, most with a matching filled state.

Elevation

6 shadow levels, from flush to system-level, each bound to the Shadow/Ambient and Shadow/Key tokens.

Layout grids

4 responsive column grids — Mobile, Tablet, Laptop, Desktop — with gutter and margin bound to Spacing tokens.

Divider

A note on theme

Every component reads its color from tokens, not hardcoded values — that's what lets this whole site (and every Orbit component) repaint correctly in light or dark with zero extra work. Orbit opens in light mode by default; use the theme control in the top bar to switch to dark.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Always reference a semantic token (bg-brand-primary, text-danger-bold) — never a primitive step (brand-green-500) directly, so a component repaints correctly in both themes with zero extra logic
  • Pair a status background with its matching status text token — bg-positive-subtle with text-positive-bold — never with text-default-primary
  • Reach for an Interactive token when the color is doing a functional job (a button, a focus ring); reserve Brand for identity moments like the logo or a hero splash
Don’t
  • Don’t hardcode a hex value anywhere, even one that looks theme-independent — bg-default-primary is #FFFFFF in light and #1E1E1E in dark, so a literal #FFFFFF silently breaks dark mode
  • Don’t invert a dark-mode color by flipping lightness — Orbit’s dark values are separately authored, not computed
  • Don’t reach for Bold when Subtle or Subtlest would do — match the token’s emphasis to how much attention the message actually deserves

Usage guidelines

Semantic vs. primitive

Components only ever reference a semantic token (bg-brand-primary, text-danger-bold) — never a primitive step (brand-green-500) directly. The semantic layer is what lets a single component render correctly in both themes without any per-component dark-mode logic.

Dark mode is a remap, not an invert

Dark-mode values are separately authored, not computed. Brand green text moves from Brand Green 500 (#86BC25) to Brand Green 300 (#C3DE92) — a lighter step on the same ramp — so it keeps enough contrast against a near-black surface instead of just inverting lightness.

Pair status tokens together

A status background always pairs with its matching status text token — bg-positive-subtle with text-positive-bold, bg-danger-subtle with text-danger-bold — never with text-default-primary, which isn’t tuned for contrast against a tinted background.

Bold vs. Subtle vs. Subtlest

Within Positive, Warning, Danger, and Info, Bold is the saturated, high-emphasis step (a solid badge or button); Subtle and Subtlest are progressively lower-emphasis tinted surfaces (a banner or inline hint) — pick by how much attention the message deserves, not by availability.

Interactive is not Brand

Brand colors identify Orbit/the product. Interactive colors (bg-interactive-primary, border-focus-default) drive actual clickable affordances — buttons, links, focus rings. They often share a hue, but a component should reach for Interactive, not Brand, when the color is doing a functional job.

Never hardcode a hex value

Even a color that looks static (pure white, pure black) should read from a token — bg-default-primary is #FFFFFF in light mode and #1E1E1E in dark, so a hardcoded #FFFFFF silently breaks in dark mode.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Match a text style to its role, not just its pixel size — a small heading still uses a Title step, never a Body size styled to look small
  • Cap font-weight at 500 everywhere; browsers default h1–h3 to bold, so override that explicitly
  • Let tracking open up as size shrinks — Body/Label Small earns more letter-spacing than Display Large, which is intentional, not an inconsistency to flatten
Don’t
  • Don’t use Display sizes (36–57px) for anything other than a marketing-style hero — they read as too heavy for an in-product page title
  • Don’t style a heading in a Body size just because it should look visually small — reach for a Title step instead
  • Don’t mix font families — Inter carries every UI string; JetBrains Mono is reserved for genuine code, identifiers, or data values

Usage guidelines

Display — hero moments only

Display Large/Medium/Small (36–57px) are reserved for marketing-style hero headings. They’re too heavy for in-product page titles.

Headline — page and section titles

Headline Large/Medium/Small (24–32px) mark page titles and major section breaks inside a product surface — the level below a marketing hero.

Title — card and control headers

Title Large/Medium/Small (14–22px) label a card, dialog, or a control’s own heading — Title Medium and Small step up to weight 500, unlike every larger step which stays at 400.

Body — paragraph copy

Body Large/Medium/Small (12–16px) is for actual reading copy — descriptions, help text, table cells. Never style a heading in a Body size; use a Title step instead even if you want it visually small.

Label — buttons and compact UI

Label Large/Medium/Small (12–14px, weight 500) is for the text inside interactive controls — buttons, tags, toasts’ action text — not for prose.

Tracking opens up as size shrinks

Letter-spacing runs from -0.25px at Display Large to +0.4–0.5px at Body/Label Small. Smaller text is intentionally given more room between letters to stay legible; don’t flatten every size to the same tracking value.

Spacing & radius

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Pick a spacing token by the role it plays — space-3xs/2xs for icon-to-label gaps, space-md/lg for card padding, space-xl and up for page-level layout — not by whichever number happens to look close
  • Use corner-full (1000px) for anything that should read as a pill or a dot — toggle tracks, pagination buttons — never a large-but-finite radius instead
  • Keep padding and gap values on the shared 9-step scale so a future token change propagates everywhere at once
Don’t
  • Don’t hand-pick an arbitrary pixel value for a padding or a gap when a token already covers that role — it silently drifts from the rest of the system the next time the scale changes
  • Don’t apply corner-lg/xl to a small compact control like a chip or a button — reserve the larger radii for cards and panels
  • Don’t treat the corner-radius and spacing scales as interchangeable — a radius token sizes a corner, a spacing token sizes a gap

Usage guidelines

space-3xs / space-2xs — icon-to-label gaps

2–4px, for the smallest gaps: an icon sitting next to its label, or a badge hugging text.

space-xs / space-sm — internal control padding

8–12px, used inside compact controls — the gap in Orbit’s own toolbar and pill-shaped nav buttons, or a checkbox’s label-to-subtext spacing.

space-md / space-lg — card padding and stacked content

16–24px, the default padding for a card or panel, and the vertical rhythm between stacked rows inside one (e.g. a settings list).

space-xl and up — page-level layout

32px and above, for gaps between major sections of a page rather than anything inside a single component.

corner-xs / corner-sm — buttons and compact controls

4–8px. Orbit’s own tooltip trigger buttons round at 8px (corner-sm).

corner-md / corner-lg — cards and panels

12–16px. The toolbar and quick-link cards on this site round at 10px, in this range.

corner-full — pills and toggles

1000px (i.e. fully round). Used for the Toggle Switch track/thumb and Pagination’s circular page buttons — anything that should read as a pill or a dot, not a rounded rectangle.

FOUNDATIONS

Iconography

73 glyphs, each bound to the icon-* color tokens. Most icons have a matching filled state for the "on" reading of a control; directional icons (chevron, arrow) instead ship one glyph per direction.

Library

Click any icon to copy its SVG markup. Search matches the icon name and common synonyms (e.g. "eye" finds visibility, "trash" finds delete).

No icons match "".

Naming convention

Names are kebab-case and describe meaning or action, not shape — content-copy, more-horizontal, self-improvement. A filled variant reuses the same base name with a -filled suffix (check-circle → check-circle-filled).

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use the filled variant to represent the active/selected/unread reading of a control (check-circle-filled, notification-filled), and the outline version for its neutral, resting state
  • Bind an icon’s color to an icon-* token, the same semantic layer as everything else, never a hardcoded fill
  • Search the library by concept or synonym before assuming a new glyph is needed
Don’t
  • Don’t stretch or skew an icon off its native 24×24 canvas — every glyph is drawn at that size so it drops into a layout at a consistent optical weight
  • Don’t invent a new icon for a concept the library already covers under a different name
  • Don’t give close a solid fill — it’s the one documented exception, drawn as open stroked lines; forcing a fill paints nothing

Usage guidelines

24×24 canvas, always

Every glyph is drawn on the same 24×24 viewBox so icons drop into a layout at a consistent optical size without per-icon adjustment.

Filled variants mean "on"

An icon with a filled counterpart (check-circle → check-circle-filled, notification → notification-filled) uses the filled version to represent the active/selected/unread reading of a control, and the outline version for its neutral state.

Fill by default, stroke by exception

Icons render as a solid currentColor fill. The one documented exception is close, whose glyph is two open line segments with no enclosed area — it has to render with stroke instead, or it paints nothing at all.

Color always comes from a token

An icon’s color is bound to an icon-* token (e.g. icon-disabled), the same semantic layer as everything else on this page — never a hardcoded fill color.

FOUNDATIONS

Elevation

6 shadow levels, Level 0 through Level 5, each stacking an ambient and a key shadow bound to the Shadow/Ambient and Shadow/Key tokens — never a hand-picked shadow color.

Levels

Elevation/Level 0Background level
Elevation/Level 1Cards, Pressed buttons
Elevation/Level 2Buttons, Notification badges
Elevation/Level 3Navigation, App bars
Elevation/Level 4Raised cards & buttons
Elevation/Level 5Modals, Pickers, popovers

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use elevation to signal real hierarchy — dialogs, menus, tooltips above content, never as decoration.
  • Raise a surface only while it temporarily separates from the layout (popover, dropdown, floating action).
  • Pair a higher level with a plain, light surface so the shadow stays legible.
Don’t
  • Don’t apply a high level to static, in-flow content like list cards — keep those at Level 1–2.
  • Don’t hand-stack multiple shadows — apply a single Elevation style per surface.
  • Don’t rely on elevation alone to signal interactivity — pair it with color or border too.

Usage guidelines

Level 0 — flush

No shadow at all — the resting state for content that sits flush with the page, like a full-width section or a static background panel.

Level 1–2 — resting UI

A subtle lift for cards, list rows, and other in-flow surfaces that sit slightly above the page background without detaching from the layout.

Level 3 — floating overlays

Dropdowns, menus, tooltips, and popovers — anything that temporarily floats above the layout and disappears once the interaction ends.

Level 4 — modals & dialogs

Content that blocks and sits above the entire page, like a modal or dialog, paired with a scrim to reinforce the separation.

Level 5 — system-level surfaces

Reserved for the rare surface that must sit above everything else, including open dialogs — a system alert or global overlay. Use sparingly; stacking more than one defeats the purpose.

FOUNDATIONS

Layout grids

4 responsive column grids — Mobile (S), Tablet (M), Laptop (L), Desktop (XL) — all Stretch-aligned, with gutter and margin bound to the Spacing scale.

Breakpoints

Mobile (S)≥ 360px · 4 columns · 16px gutter (Spacing/md) · 16px margin (Spacing/md)
Tablet (M)≥ 600px · 8 columns · 24px gutter (Spacing/lg) · 24px margin (Spacing/lg)
Laptop (L)≥ 1024px · 12 columns · 24px gutter (Spacing/lg) · 32px margin (Spacing/xl)
Desktop (XL)≥ 1440px · 12 columns · 32px gutter (Spacing/xl) · 64px margin (Spacing/3xl)

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Match the Layout Grid to the actual breakpoint being designed — Mobile (S), Tablet (M), Laptop (L), or Desktop (XL) — not just whichever one looks close.
  • Let column count and gutter scale together as the viewport grows, rather than stretching a fixed grid to fit.
  • Keep margins bound to the Spacing tokens so they stay in sync if the scale ever changes.
Don’t
  • Don’t hand-draw column guides — always apply the matching Layout Grid style so it stays linked to the shared Spacing tokens.
  • Don’t mix breakpoint grids within the same layout, like a Desktop grid on a Tablet-sized frame.
  • Don’t treat the grid as decorative — content should actually align to its columns, not just float on top of it.

Usage guidelines

Mobile (S)

4 columns, 16px gutter, 16px margin (Spacing/md). For phone-width viewports and the narrowest layouts.

Tablet (M)

8 columns, 24px gutter, 24px margin (Spacing/lg). For tablet-width and small-window layouts.

Laptop (L)

12 columns, 24px gutter, 32px margin (Spacing/xl). The standard desktop working width.

Desktop (XL)

12 columns, 32px gutter, 64px margin (Spacing/3xl) — the same column count as Laptop, but with more breathing room for wide monitors and marketing-scale layouts.

Choosing a breakpoint

Design at the breakpoint’s actual viewport width, not a scaled-down proxy, and re-check the layout at the adjacent breakpoints before shipping — content that only works at one exact width will break at the next.

Applying a grid style

Apply a style from the Layout Grid panel (right sidebar → Layout grid → +) rather than drawing columns manually. All four use alignment "Stretch", so columns resize fluidly as the frame is resized. Gutter and margin are bound to Orbit’s Spacing tokens — changing a token updates every grid style that references it.

COMPONENTS

Checkbox

Independent, multi-select choices — never interchangeable with a Radio Button.

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Box — the 24px indicator, with a 2px ring on keyboard focus
  2. 2Label — a clickable title, with optional subtext beneath it

Options

labeltext / nonedefault: none

When no label is set, the checkbox renders standalone — reserve this for dense contexts like a table cell where a column header already states the meaning.

subtexttext / nonedefault: none

Optional supporting copy under the label, for when the title alone needs a bit more context.

selectedyes / nodefault: no

Whether the box shows the filled, checked state.

indeterminateyes / nodefault: no

A display-only state for a parent checkbox whose children are partially selected. It overrides selected — never a third state a person sets by clicking.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Removes interaction but keeps the option visible, so layout and context are preserved.

States

Default
Selected
Indeterminate

Behaviors

  • Hover shifts the box to icon-default-secondary; it does not change the checked state.
  • Keyboard focus adds a 2px ring around the box, in the same hue family as the box itself, without altering hover styling.
  • The label wraps onto a second line when the available width is too narrow, rather than truncating.
  • Clicking anywhere in the label — not just the 24px box — toggles the checkbox, since the label sits inside the same clickable element.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use checkboxes for independent, multi-select choices — never for options where only one can be true
  • Use Indeterminate only to show a parent whose children are partially selected
  • Keep the label clickable to enlarge the tap target
Don’t
  • Don’t use a checkbox when only one option can be selected — use a radio button instead
  • Don’t rely on color alone to show selection — the checkmark must stay visible
  • Don’t disable a checkbox without a nearby reason why

Usage guidelines

Checkbox vs. Radio Button

Use Checkbox when a person can pick zero, one, or many options independently. Use Radio Button when exactly one option must be chosen from a set — the two controls are not interchangeable.

Selected vs. Indeterminate

Selected means the option is fully checked. Indeterminate is a display-only state for a parent checkbox whose child items are partially selected — never a third value a person clicks into directly.

With label vs. without

With a label is the default: it enlarges the click target and is required for accessibility. Without a label only fits dense contexts like table cells where a column header already states the meaning.

Focused vs. Hover

Focused appears only via keyboard navigation and must stay visible for accessibility. Hover only appears on pointer devices — don’t treat the two as equivalent.

Disabled state

Use Disabled when the option truly can’t be interacted with right now, and pair it with nearby supporting text explaining why whenever the reason isn’t obvious from context.

Keyboard interactions

SpaceToggles between selected and not selected. If the checkbox started indeterminate, the first toggle selects it.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the checkbox, in document order.

Code

<Checkbox
  label="Email alerts"
  checked={checked}
  onChange={setChecked}
/>

<Checkbox
  label="All notifications"
  checked={allChecked}
  indeterminate={someChecked}
  onChange={toggleAll}
/>

Radio Button

Exactly one option from a visible, mutually exclusive set.

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Circle — the 24px indicator, with a 2px ring on keyboard focus
  2. 2Label — a clickable title

Options

labeltext / nonedefault: none

When no label is set, the radio renders standalone — reserve this for dense contexts like a table cell where a column header already states the meaning.

selectedyes / nodefault: no

Exactly one radio in a group should be selected at a time; selecting one clears any other in the same group automatically.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Removes interaction from a single option but keeps it visible, so layout and context are preserved.

States

Unselected
Selected

Behaviors

  • Hover shifts the circle to icon-default-secondary; it does not change selection.
  • Keyboard focus adds a 2px ring around the circle without altering hover styling.
  • Selecting one radio in a group deselects whichever option was previously selected in that same group — enforced by sharing one native input name.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Radio Button only when exactly one option must be chosen from a visible, mutually exclusive set
  • Set a sensible default selection so the group isn’t left with nothing chosen, unless "none" is a valid choice
  • Keep the label clickable to enlarge the tap target
Don’t
  • Don’t use Radio Buttons for independent, multi-select choices — use checkboxes instead
  • Don’t hide a small set of mutually exclusive options behind a dropdown — radio buttons work best when all choices are visible at once
  • Don’t disable a single option in a group without a nearby reason why

Usage guidelines

Radio Button vs. Checkbox

Use Radio Button when exactly one option must be chosen from a mutually exclusive set. Use Checkbox when a person can pick zero, one, or many options independently — the two controls are not interchangeable.

With label vs. without

With a label is the default: it enlarges the click target and is required for accessibility. Without a label only fits dense contexts like table cells where a column header already states the meaning.

Focused vs. Hover

Focused appears only via keyboard navigation and must stay visible for accessibility. Hover only appears on pointer devices — don’t treat the two as equivalent.

Selected state

Exactly one radio button in a group should be selected at a time. Set a sensible default whenever possible so the group isn’t left with no option chosen.

Disabled state

Use Disabled when an option truly can’t be chosen right now, and pair it with nearby supporting text explaining why whenever the reason isn’t obvious from context.

Keyboard interactions

↑ or ↓ or ← or →Moves selection to the previous or next option within the same group.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves focus into or out of the whole group as a unit, not between individual options.

Code

<RadioGroup
  legend="Choose a shipping method"
  options={[
    { value: 'standard', label: 'Standard (5–7 days)' },
    { value: 'express', label: 'Express (2–3 days)' },
    { value: 'overnight', label: 'Overnight' },
  ]}
  value={value}
  onChange={setValue}
/>

Toggle Switch

A binary setting that takes effect immediately, with no separate save step.

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Label — a short, single-purpose description
  2. 2Track & thumb — pill background and sliding indicator, colored by state

Options

labeltextdefault: —

A short, single-purpose description of what turns on or off. Always pair the switch with one — never present it without context.

sizesmall / mediumdefault: medium

Small suits dense settings lists and table rows. Medium is the default for standalone settings screens and forms.

checkedyes / nodefault: no

Active means the setting is on and takes effect immediately; there is no intermediate or pending state.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Use when the setting can’t be changed right now, such as when a dependency or permission isn’t met — not simply to represent an off value.

States

small
medium

Behaviors

  • Toggling slides the thumb to the opposite edge and swaps the track color in one motion — position and color always agree.
  • Keyboard focus draws an outline ring around the track without moving the thumb.
  • The click target is the whole label-plus-switch row, not just the 44×24 (or 32×18) control itself.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use a toggle switch for a setting that takes effect immediately, with no separate save or confirm step
  • Pair the switch with a clear, single-purpose label so the on/off meaning is unambiguous
  • Choose Small for dense settings lists and Medium as the default for standalone settings screens
Don’t
  • Don’t use a toggle switch for actions that need confirmation or are destructive — use a button instead
  • Don’t use a toggle switch when users must choose one of three or more options — use radio buttons instead
  • Don’t rely on color alone to show state — the switch’s position must always convey on vs. off

Usage guidelines

Active vs. Inactive

Active means the setting is currently on and takes effect immediately; Inactive means it’s off. There is no intermediate or pending state.

Size scale

Small suits dense settings lists and table rows. Medium is the default for standalone settings screens and forms.

Toggle vs. Checkbox

Use a Toggle Switch for a single binary setting that applies right away. Use a Checkbox when the choice is part of a form with an explicit save step, or when selecting multiple independent options.

Disabled state

Use Disabled when the setting can’t be changed right now, such as when a dependency or permission isn’t met — not simply to represent an off value.

Labeling

Always pair the switch with a short, descriptive label stating what turns on or off; never present a switch without that context.

Keyboard interactions

SpaceToggles between active and inactive.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the switch.

Code

<ToggleSwitch
  label="Push notifications"
  checked={checked}
  onChange={setChecked}
/>

Tooltip

Brief, supplementary text shown on hover or keyboard focus.

Copy to clipboard

Anatomy

12
Copy
  1. 1Bubble & arrow — label text on an inverse-colored chip, pointing back at the anchor
  2. 2Anchor — the element being described

Options

labeltextdefault: —

One short phrase describing the anchor’s purpose — never a multi-sentence explanation.

placementtop / bottom / left / rightdefault: top

Chosen based on the space available around the anchor; flip to the opposite side when the default direction would run off-screen.

showArrowyes / nodefault: yes

Keep the arrow on to visually connect the tooltip to its anchor. Hide it only when the anchor is unambiguous, such as inside a dense toolbar.

States

Tooltip textTooltip textTooltip textTooltip text

Behaviors

  • Appears on both pointer hover and keyboard focus of the anchor, so keyboard-only users see the same information.
  • Disappears the instant the pointer leaves the anchor or focus moves elsewhere — there is no manual dismiss.
  • Never delays before appearing; the moment hover or focus lands on the anchor, the tooltip is shown.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use a tooltip for brief, supplementary text that isn’t essential to completing the task
  • Choose the Placement (Top, Bottom, Left, Right) that keeps the tooltip clear of nearby content and viewport edges
  • Keep the arrow visible when the tooltip needs a clear visual link back to its anchor element
Don’t
  • Don’t put interactive elements like links, buttons, or form fields inside a tooltip — it disappears as soon as hover or focus is lost
  • Don’t use a tooltip to convey critical or error information the user must see — surface that inline instead
  • Don’t write long paragraphs — keep the label to a short phrase since the tooltip only shows briefly

Usage guidelines

Placement

Choose Top, Bottom, Left, or Right based on the space available around the anchor, and flip to the opposite side when the default direction would run off-screen.

Trigger & dismissal

A tooltip appears on hover or keyboard focus of its anchor element and disappears as soon as the pointer leaves or focus moves elsewhere.

Show Arrow

Keep the arrow on to visually connect the tooltip to its anchor. Hide it only when the anchor is unambiguous, such as inside a dense toolbar.

Label content

Keep the label to one short phrase describing the anchor’s purpose — tooltips aren’t meant for multi-sentence explanations.

When not to use

Skip the tooltip if the anchor already has a visible text label, or if the information is necessary to complete the task — surface it inline instead.

Keyboard interactions

TabMoves focus onto the anchor element, which reveals its tooltip.
Shift+TabMoves focus away from the anchor, which hides the tooltip.

Code

<Tooltip label="Copy" placement="top">
  <IconButton icon="content-copy" aria-label="Copy" />
</Tooltip>

COMPONENTS

Pagination

Navigation across a long list of pages, with the current position always visible.

Anatomy

123
…
  1. 1Previous / Next — one-page-at-a-time chevrons
  2. 2Ellipsis — visual truncation, not a menu
  3. 3Page number — filled when current

Options

pagenumberdefault: —

The current page — drives which page-number button renders filled.

totalPagesnumberdefault: —

The total page count the range and Next boundary are computed from.

sizesmall / medium / largedefault: medium

Small fits dense tables and compact toolbars. Medium is the default for most content lists. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

States

Behaviors

  • Clicking a page number, or Previous/Next, immediately recomputes the collapsed range around the new current page.
  • Previous disables itself on page 1; Next disables itself on the last page — never both at once, since at least one direction should stay reachable unless there truly is only one page.
  • The ellipsis never receives focus or a click handler — it is a visual truncation only.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use numbered pagination when users need to jump directly to a page, and the Stepper variant when they only move one page at a time
  • Keep Prev/Next chevrons visible even when page numbers are shown, for consistent sequential navigation
  • Collapse long page ranges with an ellipsis instead of listing every number
Don’t
  • Don’t disable both Prev and Next at once — at least one direction should stay enabled unless there’s truly only one page
  • Don’t rely on the Current-page style alone to convey position — pair it with a visible page count when possible
  • Don’t switch between numbered pagination and the Stepper mid-flow

Usage guidelines

Numbered vs. Stepper

Use full numbered pagination when the total page count is visible and people benefit from jumping directly to a page. Use a Stepper ("1 of 7") when space is tight or pages are only ever visited in sequence.

Size scale

Small fits dense tables and compact toolbars. Medium is the default for most content lists. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

Ellipsis

Insert the ellipsis once a page range would otherwise show more numbers than fit comfortably. It’s a visual truncation only, not an interactive jump-to-any-page menu.

Current vs. Focused

Current marks the page a person is actively viewing and persists regardless of input method. Focused only appears during keyboard navigation and moves independently of the Current page.

Disabled state

Disable a direction or a specific page number only when moving there is genuinely impossible right now, such as being on the first or last page.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves focus between Previous, each page number, and Next, in visual order.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused button, navigating to that page.

Code

<Pagination
  page={page}
  totalPages={22}
  onPageChange={setPage}
/>

Toast

A short-lived message that disappears on its own — never a home for anything critical.

Changes savedYour changes have been saved successfully.

Anatomy

1234
Changes savedYour changes have been saved.
  1. 1Icon — reinforces the type
  2. 2Title & description — headline plus optional copy
  3. 3Action — optional time-sensitive follow-up
  4. 4Close — optional manual dismiss

Options

typesuccess / warning / danger / infodefault: success

Matches the message’s intent so color and icon reinforce meaning — never chosen for decoration.

titletextdefault: —

A short headline, scannable at a glance.

descriptiontext / nonedefault: none

Turn this on when the title alone doesn’t give enough context, such as naming what specifically failed or changed.

onActionhandler / nonedefault: none

Enable only for a real, time-sensitive follow-up like Undo or Retry — not as a generic link to more information.

onClosehandler / nonedefault: none

Show on toasts that may stay on screen longer or that people may want to dismiss early; quick auto-dismissing confirmations can often skip it.

States

Behaviors

  • New toasts stack below existing ones and animate in from above.
  • Each toast auto-dismisses on its own five-second timer, independent of any others on screen.
  • Clicking Undo or Close removes only that toast immediately, without waiting for its timer.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use the Type that matches the message’s intent — Success, Warning, Danger, or Info — so color and icon reinforce meaning
  • Show an Action only when there’s a real, time-sensitive follow-up like Undo or Retry
  • Keep the message short enough to scan at a glance, adding Description only when necessary context won’t fit in the title
Don’t
  • Don’t use Danger for anything other than a failure or destructive outcome that needs immediate attention
  • Don’t stack an Action and a Close on every toast — only add what the message actually needs
  • Don’t rely on a toast for information the user must not miss, since it disappears on its own

Usage guidelines

Toast type

Use Success, Warning, Danger, or Info to match the message’s intent — color and icon should always reflect what’s actually happening.

Description

Turn on the description when the title alone doesn’t give enough context, such as naming what specifically failed or changed.

Action

Enable an action only for a real, time-sensitive follow-up like Undo or Retry — not as a generic link to more information.

Close control

Show Close on toasts that may stay on screen longer or that people may want to dismiss early; quick auto-dismissing confirmations can often skip it.

Dismissal & timing

Toasts disappear on their own after a few seconds, so never put information a person absolutely must read in one — use a dialog or inline message instead.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves focus to the Undo action or Close control when either is present.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused control.

Code

<Toast
  type="success"
  title="Changes saved"
  description="Your changes have been saved successfully."
  onAction={handleUndo}
  onClose={handleDismiss}
/>

Button

Triggers a single action or event, in Primary, Secondary, or Tertiary emphasis.

Anatomy

123
  1. 1Container — the filled or transparent background, sized by Size and rounded by Shape
  2. 2Icon — optional, leading the label, reinforcing its meaning
  3. 3Label — the action’s name, always present

Options

typePrimary / Secondary / Tertiarydefault: Primary

Primary marks the single most important action in a view. Secondary supports it, like "Cancel" next to "Save." Tertiary is for low-emphasis or optional actions, like an inline link styled as a button.

shapeRound / Squaredefault: Round

Both carry equal visual weight — the choice is a brand and layout preference, not a meaning difference. Keep it consistent within a single flow rather than switching between them from screen to screen.

sizeXSmall / Small / Medium / Large / XLargedefault: Medium

XSmall and Small fit dense toolbars and inline table actions. Medium is the default for most forms and dialogs. Large and XLarge suit touch-first or high-emphasis moments, like an empty-state call-to-action.

iconleading icon / nonedefault: none

Add a leading icon only when it reinforces the label’s meaning, like a download icon on "Download." A decorative icon adds visual noise without adding information.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Disable a button only when the action truly cannot be completed right now, and make the reason discoverable nearby — a disabled button with no explanation reads as a bug.

States

Primary
Secondary
Tertiary

Behaviors

  • Hover darkens Primary and Secondary’s fill by one step, and tints Tertiary’s background without changing its transparent-by-default look.
  • Pressed moves one step further than Hover in the same direction, giving tactile feedback that the click registered.
  • Keyboard focus shows a visible ring in the same hue family as the button, without altering its hover styling.
  • Disabled removes the fill’s emphasis and switches the label to a muted tone, while keeping the button’s size and position in layout.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Primary for the single most important action in a view; reserve Secondary and Tertiary for supporting or lower-emphasis actions
  • Keep one Primary button per view — competing primary actions confuse the hierarchy
  • Keep Shape (Round/Square) consistent within a single screen or flow
Don’t
  • Don’t use Tertiary for an action the user must not miss — its low visual weight is meant for optional actions
  • Don’t show an icon without a label unless its meaning is already universal, like a close X
  • Don’t disable a button without a nearby explanation of what’s needed to enable it

Usage guidelines

Primary vs. Secondary vs. Tertiary

Primary marks the single most important action in a view. Secondary supports it, like "Cancel" next to "Save." Tertiary is for low-emphasis or optional actions, like an inline link styled as a button.

Round vs. Square

Both carry equal visual weight — the choice is a brand and layout preference, not a meaning difference. Keep it consistent within a single flow rather than switching between them from screen to screen.

Size scale

XSmall and Small fit dense toolbars and inline table actions. Medium is the default for most forms and dialogs. Large and XLarge suit touch-first or high-emphasis moments, like an empty-state call-to-action.

Show icon

Add a leading icon only when it reinforces the label’s meaning, like a download icon on "Download." A decorative icon adds visual noise without adding information.

Disabled state

Disable a button only when the action truly cannot be completed right now, and make the reason discoverable nearby — a disabled button with no explanation reads as a bug.

Keyboard interactions

Enter or SpaceActivates the focused button.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the button, in document order.

Code

<Button type="primary" shape="round" size="medium" onClick={handleSave}>
  Save changes
</Button>

<Button type="tertiary" shape="round" size="small" disabled>
  Cancel
</Button>

COMPONENTS

Text Input

The shared field primitive for a single line of text — label, input pill, and supporting text.

EmailWe’ll never share your email.

Anatomy

123
LabelSupporting text
  1. 1Label — sits above the field, always visible (never placeholder-only)
  2. 2Field — the bordered input pill, with optional leading/trailing icon slots
  3. 3Supporting text — helper copy or an error message below the field

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Medium is the default for most forms. Small suits dense layouts and inline table edits. Large works for a single, high-emphasis field such as a landing-page search or signup.

labeltextdefault: —

Always shown near the field, never used as the only cue — placeholder text disappears once a person starts typing.

supportingTexttext / nonedefault: none

Helper copy under the field, or the explanatory message that must accompany an Error state.

iconleading / trailing / nonedefault: none

Turn on an icon only when it adds real meaning (search, password, currency) — it is off by default. The clear icon appears automatically once a field is Filled; the error icon appears automatically in the Error state.

stateEnabled / Hover / Focused / Filled / Error / Disableddefault: Enabled

Filled shows a real value has been entered, distinct from placeholder text in Enabled. Error pairs a colored border and icon with an explanatory message. Disabled means the field cannot be edited right now.

States

Behaviors

  • Hover darkens the field’s background by one step; it does not change the border.
  • Focus switches the border to a 2px teal ring and keeps it visible for the duration of keyboard editing — never suppressed for visual cleanliness.
  • Error switches the border and label/supporting text to a danger color, and must always be paired with an explanatory supporting-text message, not color alone.
  • Disabled mutes the field’s background, border stays, and the label/value switch to a muted tone.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Pair every field with a visible label, near the field, not just placeholder text
  • Show the leading icon only when it adds real meaning (search, password, currency) — leave it off otherwise
  • Let the clear button appear once a field has content, not before
  • Use Textarea instead of stretching Text Field for anything longer than a line
Don’t
  • Don’t use placeholder text as the only label — it disappears once the user starts typing
  • Don’t show an error without a supporting-text explanation of what to fix
  • Don’t disable a field without saying why nearby
  • Don’t give Compose Bar a visible label — its container (chat thread, channel) already provides that context

Usage guidelines

Text Input vs. Compose Bar

These are the same Text Field component, just configured differently. Text Input: label + supporting text on, leading icon off. Compose Bar: label/supporting off, leading = attach, trailing = voice + send.

Text Field vs. Textarea

Use Text Field for a single value that fits on one line (name, email, search). Use Textarea once the content is expected to wrap — comments, descriptions, notes.

Size scale

Medium is the default for most forms. Small suits dense layouts and inline table edits. Large works for a single, high-emphasis field such as a landing-page search or signup.

Leading & trailing icons

Turn on a leading icon only when it adds real meaning (search, password, currency) — it is off by default. The clear icon appears automatically once a field is Filled; the error icon appears automatically in the Error state.

Filled / Error / Disabled

Filled shows a real value has been entered, distinct from placeholder text in Enabled. Error pairs a colored border and icon with an explanatory message — never rely on color alone. Disabled means the field cannot be edited right now, not just discouraged.

Accessibility

Pair the Error state with icon + text, not color alone. Placeholder and supporting text are bound to Text/Default/Secondary (not Tertiary) to clear the 4.5:1 text-contrast minimum in both Light and Dark mode. Keep the focus ring visible — never suppress it for visual cleanliness.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the field, in document order.
EscapeClears the field when a clear (trailing) icon is present and the field has focus.

Code

<TextInput
  label="Email"
  value={email}
  onChange={setEmail}
  supportingText={error ? "Enter a valid email address" : undefined}
  error={!!error}
/>

AnatomyOptionsStatesBehaviorsDo’s & Don’tsUsage guidelinesKeyboard interactionsCode
COMPONENTS

Search

A dedicated search input — a pill-shaped field with a leading search icon, sized Small/Medium/Large, that swaps its trailing icon automatically between a clear affordance and an error indicator.

No results found. Try a different search term.

Anatomy

1234
Design system
No results found. Try a different search term.
  1. 1Leading icon — the search glyph, on by default
  2. 2Input text — placeholder or an entered value, always in the same primary ink color
  3. 3Trailing icon — appears automatically: a clear (✕) icon once Filled, or an error icon in the Error state
  4. 4Supporting text — an explanatory error message, Error state only

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Small (36px, 16px icon) fits compact contexts like toolbars and filter bars. Medium (48px, 20px icon) is the default for most page-level search. Large (56px, 24px icon) works best as a primary, high-emphasis entry point such as a search landing page.

show icontrue / falsedefault: true

Keep the search icon visible by default — it signals the field's purpose at a glance. Turn it off only when space is tight and the field's placement or label already makes its purpose obvious.

stateEnabled / Hover / Focused / Filled / Error / Disableddefault: Enabled

Filled shows a real entered value and reveals a trailing clear icon. Error swaps the border and trailing icon to a danger treatment and must be paired with supporting text explaining what went wrong.

States

Behaviors

  • Hover darkens the field's background by one step (Background/Default/Secondary Hover); the border doesn't change.
  • Focused switches to a 2px Background/Interactive/Primary border — kept visible for the duration of keyboard editing.
  • Filled reveals a trailing clear (✕) icon once real text is present, replacing the empty trailing space — clicking it should clear the field.
  • Error swaps the border to Border/Danger/Subtle, swaps the trailing icon from clear to an error glyph, and must show supporting text explaining the problem — never color alone.
  • Disabled mutes the background to Background/Disabled/Default, keeps a Border/Default/Primary border (not a distinct disabled border token), and mutes the text to Text/Disabled/Default.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Show the search icon by default so the field's purpose is clear at a glance
  • Use the Results Dropdown's Suggestions or Recent state to help users find what they need faster
  • Pair the Error state with a message explaining what went wrong or what to try instead
Don’t
  • Don't remove the search icon unless the field's purpose is already obvious from a nearby label
  • Don't leave the field in a Loading state longer than necessary — show results or an Empty state as soon as you can
  • Don't disable the field without a nearby reason why

Usage guidelines

Small / Medium / Large

Small fits compact contexts like toolbars and filter bars. Medium is the default for most page-level search. Large works best as a primary, high-emphasis entry point such as a search landing page.

Show Icon

Keep the search icon visible by default — it signals the field's purpose at a glance. Turn it off only when space is tight and the field's placement or label already makes its purpose obvious.

Suggestions / Recent

Use Suggestions to surface likely matches as the user types. Use Recent to show their past searches when the field is focused but empty — don't show both at once.

Loading / Empty

Loading appears briefly while results are being fetched. Empty tells the user their query returned nothing — pair it with a suggestion for what to try next.

Error / Disabled

Use Error when the query itself is invalid and explain why nearby. Use Disabled when search isn't available yet, not as a way to discourage use.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the field, in document order.
EscapeClears the field when it has focus and a value is present.
EnterSubmits the current query.

Code

<Search
  size="medium"
  value={query}
  onChange={setQuery}
  error={hasError}
  supportingText={hasError ? "No results found. Try a different search term." : undefined}
/>

COMPONENTS

Textarea

A multi-line text field for content expected to wrap — comments, descriptions, notes — with the same Label/Field/Supporting-text shape as Text Input, plus an optional character counter.

Label
Supporting text0/500

Anatomy

1234
Label
Type here..
Supporting text0/500
  1. 1Label — sits above the field, on by default
  2. 2Field — the fixed-height, multi-line input box
  3. 3Supporting text — helper copy or an error message, off by default
  4. 4Counter — an optional character count (e.g. "0/500"), off by default

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Small (84px field height) suits dense layouts. Medium (104px) is the default for most forms. Large (132px) suits a single, high-emphasis field. Unlike Search, Textarea keeps the same 12px corner radius across all 3 sizes.

show labeltrue / falsedefault: true

On by default — a visible label, not placeholder text, should carry the field's purpose.

show supporting text / show countertrue / falsedefault: false / false

Both off by default and independent of each other and of State — turning either on doesn't require the other, though Error should always be paired with supporting text explaining the problem.

stateEnabled / Hover / Focused / Filled / Error / Disableddefault: Enabled

Placeholder/value text is Text/Default/Secondary in Enabled/Hover/Focused, switches to Text/Default/Primary once Filled or in Error, and to Text/Disabled/Default when Disabled.

States

Behaviors

  • Hover darkens the field's background by one step (Background/Default/Secondary Hover); the border doesn't change.
  • Focused switches to a 2px Border/Focus/Default border — kept visible for the duration of keyboard editing.
  • Filled recolors the field's text from Text/Default/Secondary to Text/Default/Primary once real content is present — Figma's own Filled variant doesn't swap in a different sample sentence, just this color change.
  • Error swaps the border to a danger color and, unlike the boolean default, ships with Supporting text already on in Figma's own documentation variant — a real content choice, not a rule that Error forces supporting text on.
  • Disabled mutes the background to Background/Disabled/Default and the text to Text/Disabled/Default; the border stays Border/Default/Primary, same as Enabled.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Textarea once content is expected to wrap — comments, descriptions, notes — instead of stretching Text Field
  • Turn on Counter for any field with a real length limit
  • Pair the Error state with supporting text explaining what to fix
Don’t
  • Don't use Textarea for a single value that fits on one line — use Text Field instead
  • Don't show an error without a supporting-text explanation
  • Don't disable the field without a nearby reason why

Usage guidelines

Text Field vs. Textarea

Use Text Field for a single value that fits on one line (name, email, search). Use Textarea once the content is expected to wrap — comments, descriptions, notes.

Size

Small suits dense layouts and inline table edits. Medium is the default for most forms. Large suits a single, high-emphasis field.

Supporting text & Counter

Both are independent, off-by-default booleans — turn on Counter for fields with a real length limit, and Supporting text for helper copy or (always, for Error) an explanatory message.

Filled / Error / Disabled

Filled shows a real value has been entered, distinct from placeholder text in Enabled. Error pairs a danger-colored border with an explanatory message — never rely on color alone. Disabled means the field cannot be edited right now.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the field, in document order.
EnterInserts a new line, rather than submitting a form — unlike a single-line Text Field.

Code

<Textarea
  label="Notes"
  value={notes}
  onChange={setNotes}
  showCounter
  maxLength={500}
  supportingText={error ? "This field is required" : undefined}
  error={!!error}
/>

COMPONENTS

Tabs

Navigation between related views within the same context and at the same level of hierarchy.

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Label — the destination’s name
  2. 2Indicator — a 2px underline marking the Selected tab

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Small suits compact toolbars and dense navigation bars. Medium is the default for standalone tab groups. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

selectedyes / nodefault: no

Exactly one tab in a group should be selected at a time — it marks which view is currently showing and persists regardless of input method.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Disable an individual tab only when its content is genuinely unavailable right now — don’t disable every tab in a group at once, since that leaves nothing to select.

States

Behaviors

  • Selecting a tab moves the 2px indicator under it and switches its label to the Interactive Primary color and weight 500.
  • Focused only appears during keyboard navigation and is independent of which tab is Selected.
  • Disabled removes interaction from a single tab and mutes both its label and indicator, but keeps it visible in the group.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Keep 3–4 tabs per group; route overflow into a menu instead of wrapping
  • Always show a clear selected-state indicator
  • Pair icons with labels when tabs support wayfinding, not decoration
Don’t
  • Don’t stack tabs onto a second row — reduce the count or add Search
  • Don’t disable every tab in a group at once
  • Don’t mix icon-only and label-only tabs in the same group

Usage guidelines

Tab count

Keep a group to 3–4 tabs for glanceable navigation. Beyond that, collapse the extra choices into an overflow menu rather than shrinking each tab or wrapping to a second row.

Icon + Label vs. Label only

Show icons alongside labels when they reinforce wayfinding — a distinct destination like Following vs. All. Drop the icon when the label alone is unambiguous, and never mix icon-only with label-only tabs in the same group.

Selected vs. Focused

Selected marks which view is currently showing and persists regardless of input method. Focused only appears during keyboard navigation and is independent of which tab is Selected.

Disabled state

Disable an individual tab only when its content is genuinely unavailable right now — don’t disable every tab in a group at once, since that leaves nothing to select.

Size scale

Small suits compact toolbars and dense navigation bars. Medium is the default for standalone tab groups. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

Keyboard interactions

Left or Right ArrowMoves focus between tabs in the group.
Enter or SpaceSelects the focused tab.
TabMoves focus out of the tab group entirely, to the next focusable element on the page.

Code

<Tabs value={activeTab} onChange={setActiveTab}>
  <Tab value="overview">Overview</Tab>
  <Tab value="activity">Activity</Tab>
  <Tab value="settings" disabled>Settings</Tab>
</Tabs>

Divider

Separates and groups related content within a layout, without adding extra visual weight.

Content above

Content left

Content below

Content right

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Line — a 1px hairline in Border/Default/Primary
  2. 2Padding — the space above and below (Horizontal) or beside (Vertical) the line, matching Orbit’s spacing scale

Options

orientationHorizontal / Verticaldefault: Horizontal

Match Orientation to the layout axis: Horizontal between stacked rows, Vertical between side-by-side columns.

paddingNone / Hairline / XSmall / Small / Medium / Large / XLargedefault: Small

Pick a padding size that matches the surrounding spacing scale — None and Hairline sit flush against neighboring content; larger steps read as a bigger structural break.

States

Behaviors

  • A Divider is purely visual — it carries no interaction states of its own.
  • It always spans the full width (Horizontal) or height (Vertical) of its container.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use a Divider to separate distinct, unrelated groups of content — not just to add rhythm between every item
  • Match Orientation to the layout axis: Horizontal between stacked rows, Vertical between side-by-side columns
  • Pick a Padding size that matches the surrounding spacing scale
Don’t
  • Don’t use a Divider as a substitute for proper spacing — most lists read fine with whitespace alone
  • Don’t stack multiple dividers in a row for emphasis — use a card boundary or background change instead
  • Don’t mix Hairline and heavier padding variants within the same list

Usage guidelines

Horizontal vs. Vertical

Horizontal separates stacked rows, like a list or settings panel. Vertical separates side-by-side items, like a toolbar. The two aren’t interchangeable — match the layout’s actual axis.

Padding scale

Hairline and None fit dense, low-emphasis contexts like table rows. Small (Default) covers most lists and cards. Medium through XLarge add breathing room between major page sections.

Divider vs. whitespace

Reach for a Divider when content needs an explicit boundary, like distinguishing unrelated groups. Rely on spacing alone when the grouping is already implied by proximity.

Cards vs. lists

Inside a card, a divider marks internal sections. Inside a list, it marks the boundary between individual items. Don’t mix both patterns inconsistently within the same surface.

Accessibility

A Divider is decorative, not structural — it should never be the only thing separating two distinct interactive regions. Pair it with real spacing and grouping in the layout itself.

Keyboard interactions

—A Divider is not interactive and never receives keyboard focus.

Code

<Divider orientation="horizontal" padding="medium" />

Chip

A compact, removable label used to categorize content, filter a list, or represent a selected input.

React

Anatomy

1234
React
  1. 1Leading icon — optional, shown before the label
  2. 2Label — the chip’s text, always present
  3. 3Border — a full-height outline, no fill by default
  4. 4Close icon — optional, shown only when the chip can be removed

Options

typePrimary / Statusdefault: Primary

Primary is interactive — it reacts to hover and pressed with a tinted fill, for filters and selectable inputs. Status is a static, neutral label for categorizing content, with no interactive fill change.

sizeX-Small / Medium / Large / X-Large / Defaultdefault: Default

X-Small suits dense filter bars; Default fits most standalone chip groups. Medium, Large, and X-Large step up the text size for higher-emphasis, touch-first contexts.

iconleading icon / nonedefault: leading icon

Add a leading icon only when it reinforces the chip’s meaning — a decorative icon adds visual noise without adding information.

closableyes / nodefault: yes

Show the close icon only when the chip can actually be removed — don’t disable it while leaving it visible.

disabledyes / nodefault: no

Removes interaction but keeps the chip visible.

States

Behaviors

  • Primary chips fill with a tinted wash on Hover and a stronger wash on Pressed; Status chips stay visually static except when Disabled.
  • Error swaps a Primary chip’s border and label to the danger color — used when a filter or selection is invalid.
  • Disabled removes interaction and mutes the border and label to a neutral gray, regardless of type.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use chips for compact, removable filters or selections — not as primary navigation or buttons
  • Keep labels short enough to read at a glance; truncate instead of wrapping to a second line
  • Show the close icon only when the chip can actually be removed
Don’t
  • Don’t use a chip group for a single mutually-exclusive choice — use a segmented control or radio group instead
  • Don’t disable the close icon while leaving it visible — remove it entirely if the chip can’t be dismissed
  • Don’t mix Primary and Status chips in the same group without a clear reason

Usage guidelines

Primary vs. Status

Use Primary chips for user-controlled filters or selections the person picked themselves. Use Status chips to communicate a system-assigned state, like a category or label, that isn’t meant to be toggled.

Size scale

X-Small and Default fit dense toolbars and tables. Medium is the standard for filter bars and forms. Large and X-Large are reserved for touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

Leading icon

Use the leading star icon only when it reinforces the chip’s meaning, like "favorited" or "featured." Omit it for plain text filters, where it would just be decoration.

Removable (close icon)

Include the close icon only when removing the chip is the point — recent searches, active filters. Leave it off when the chip is a passive label.

Error state

Use Error only to flag an invalid or conflicting selection that the user must resolve — not to indicate a negative category. That’s what a Danger-colored Status chip is for.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the chip (or its close icon, if present), in document order.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused chip or close icon.

Code

<Chip type="primary" closable onClose={handleRemove}>
  React
</Chip>

<Chip type="status">Draft</Chip>

COMPONENTS

Progress Bar

A horizontal track that communicates how far a process has run, or that one is running with an unknown duration.

Anatomy

12
  1. 1Track — the full-width base, always in Background/Default/Tertiary
  2. 2Fill — the completed portion, colored by state

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Small suits compact contexts like table rows or cards. Medium is the default for most in-page loading states. Large works best for full-width or full-screen processes where the bar is the primary focus.

stateDefault / Success / Warning / Error / Disableddefault: Default

Default represents an in-progress state with no outcome yet. Success, Warning, and Error reflect the real outcome of the tracked process — reserve them for that, not decorative variety. Disabled means the process can’t currently run.

indeterminateyes / nodefault: no

Use Indeterminate only when the duration or completion amount is unknown — its animation shows a process is running, not how far along it is. Switch to the standard determinate fill once a percentage is known.

States

Behaviors

  • Indeterminate plays a continuously animated fill with no fixed width, since there is no percentage to represent.
  • Determinate fills to a fixed width equal to the completion percentage, in the color of its current state.
  • The track color never changes across states — only the fill color and width do.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Success, Warning, and Error to reflect the real outcome of the tracked process, not for decorative variety
  • Use Indeterminate only when the duration or completion amount is unknown
  • Pair the bar with a percentage or status label when users need precision
Don’t
  • Don’t use Indeterminate for a process with a known duration or step count — use the standard determinate bar instead
  • Don’t rely on state color alone to signal success or failure for critical outcomes
  • Don’t use Disabled just to show a paused process — use it only when the process truly can’t run yet

Usage guidelines

Determinate vs. Indeterminate

Use the standard Progress Bar when completion can be calculated as a percentage. Switch to Indeterminate only when the duration or remaining work is unknown.

Small / Medium / Large

Small suits compact contexts like table rows or cards. Medium is the default for most in-page loading states. Large works best for full-width or full-screen processes where the bar is the primary focus.

Success / Warning / Error

Reserve these states for the actual outcome of the tracked process, not as decorative color variety. Default represents an in-progress state with no outcome yet.

Disabled state

Use Disabled when the process the bar represents can’t currently run or isn’t yet available, such as a step that’s locked until a prior one completes.

Pairing with labels

Add a percentage or status label nearby when users need precision, especially for longer-running or high-stakes processes — the bar alone only conveys relative progress.

Keyboard interactions

—A Progress Bar is not interactive and never receives keyboard focus.

Code

<ProgressBar size="medium" indeterminate />

<ProgressBar size="medium" state="success" value={100} />
<ProgressBar size="medium" state="warning" value={80} />
<ProgressBar size="medium" state="error" value={35} />

Breadcrumbs

A trail of links showing a person’s current location within a hierarchy, and a path back up it.

///…/

Anatomy

123
ComponentsBreadcrumbs
  1. 1Item — one level’s clickable label; only the root item may carry a leading icon
  2. 2Separator — the divider glyph (Chevron or Slash) between items
  3. 3Active item — the last, non-linked entry representing the current page

Options

items2 / 3 / 4 / Collapseddefault: 3

Use the fixed counts when the full trail fits comfortably. Switch to Collapsed once depth exceeds what the layout can show, replacing the middle items with an overflow trigger.

separatorChevron / Slashdefault: Chevron

Chevron reads as more distinctly interactive in dense product UI. Slash is a lighter, editorial style suited to content or documentation sites. Pick one per surface and keep it consistent.

iconyes / nodefault: no

Show a leading icon only on the root or home item to anchor the trail. Adding icons to every item adds visual noise without adding wayfinding value.

activeyes / nodefault: no

The last item represents the current page — set Active to yes so it’s styled as the trail’s endpoint, independent of its interactive state.

States

Behaviors

  • Hover and Pressed both recolor the item to Text/Interactive/Primary — Orbit’s Figma file defines no separate Pressed color, so the two read identically aside from cursor feedback.
  • Active recolors an item to Text/Interactive/Primary even while its own state is Enabled — the same color hover uses, since the active item is meant to read as the trail’s current, non-actionable endpoint.
  • Disabled mutes an item to Text/Disabled/Default regardless of its Active or Icon settings.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Show breadcrumbs only when a page sits at least two levels deep — skip them on top-level pages
  • Collapse long trails with the overflow menu instead of letting items wrap to a second line
  • Keep the current page as plain text, not a link — it’s the one place you can’t navigate to
Don’t
  • Don’t use breadcrumbs as the primary navigation — they supplement a nav menu or back button, not replace it
  • Don’t mix Chevron and Slash separator styles within the same trail
  • Don’t make every item a link when the trail is only 2 items

Usage guidelines

Items: 2 / 3 / 4 / Collapsed

Use the fixed counts when the full trail fits comfortably. Switch to Collapsed once depth exceeds what the layout can show, replacing the middle items with an overflow trigger.

Chevron vs. Slash

Chevron reads as more distinctly interactive in dense product UI. Slash is a lighter, editorial style suited to content or documentation sites. Pick one per surface and keep it consistent.

Icon on Breadcrumb Item

Show a leading icon only on the root or home item to anchor the trail. Adding icons to every item adds visual noise without adding wayfinding value.

Active state

The last item represents the current page — set Active=Yes so it’s styled as the trail’s endpoint, independent of its State (which still governs Enabled/Hover/Pressed/Disabled).

Overflow Trigger

Tapping it should reveal the collapsed middle items, not navigate anywhere itself — treat it as a disclosure control, not a breadcrumb link.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus between linked items, in document order. The Active (current-page) item and any Disabled item are skipped, since neither is actionable.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused item, or reveals the collapsed middle items when focus is on the overflow trigger.

Code

<Breadcrumbs separator="chevron">
  <BreadcrumbItem icon="home" href="/">Home</BreadcrumbItem>
  <BreadcrumbItem href="/components">Components</BreadcrumbItem>
  <BreadcrumbItem active>Breadcrumbs</BreadcrumbItem>
</Breadcrumbs>

Dropdown

A form field that reveals a list of options on demand, for choosing one or more values without keeping every option always visible.

Label
Option 2
Supporting text
Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
Option 4

Anatomy

12345
Label
Select an option
Supporting text
Option 1
Option 2
Option 3
  1. 1Label — describes the field, recolors to Danger on Error
  2. 2Field — the closed control: optional leading icon, value or placeholder text, and a chevron
  3. 3Menu — the option list that opens beneath the field
  4. 4Option — a single choice, in Default, Hover, Selected, or Disabled
  5. 5Supporting text — helper copy, or the required explanation under an Error

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Medium

Small suits dense forms and inline table edits. Medium is the default for most forms. Large works for a single, high-emphasis field such as a settings page or a prominent filter.

typeSingle-select / Multi-selectdefault: Single-select

Single-select closes the menu and shows the chosen value as text. Multi-select keeps the menu open for further picks and shows each selection as a removable chip in the field — turn it on only when more than one value is a genuinely valid choice.

stateEnabled / Hover / Open / Filled / Error / Disableddefault: Enabled

Open reveals the menu and flips the chevron upward; Filled shows a chosen value in place of the placeholder; Error pairs a red border and icon with required supporting text; Disabled means the field can’t be opened right now.

States

Behaviors

  • Open reveals the options menu directly beneath the field, at the same elevation as any other floating surface. The chevron flips upward and the border switches to the focus ring — never hide the menu without also flipping the chevron back down.
  • Selected options in the menu take a tinted Background/Interactive/Subtle fill so the current choice is visible without closing the menu.
  • Error pairs a red border and icon with a required supporting-text explanation — never rely on color alone.
  • Disabled means the field cannot be opened right now, not just discouraged from being changed.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use a Dropdown once there are more than about 5 options, or when space is tight — for 2–4 always-visible choices, prefer Segmented Control or Radio Buttons instead
  • Show the current selection as the field’s own value once something is chosen, not only inside the menu
  • Turn on Multi-select only when a person can genuinely choose more than one value at once
  • Pair every Error state with supporting text that explains what to fix
Don’t
  • Don’t use a Dropdown for 2–4 options that should all stay visible at once — hiding them behind a click makes the choice slower to scan than Segmented Control or Radio Buttons
  • Don’t leave the placeholder value text showing once Multi-select chips are populated — hide it so the chips get the full width
  • Don’t disable a field without saying why nearby
  • Don’t suppress the focus ring on the Open state for visual cleanliness

Usage guidelines

Dropdown vs. Segmented Control / Radio Buttons

Dropdown trades a bit of glanceability for space — the options stay hidden until opened. Use it once there are more than about 4–5 choices, or whenever the always-visible controls would crowd the layout.

Size scale

Small suits dense forms and inline table edits. Medium is the default for most forms. Large works for a single, high-emphasis field such as a settings page or a prominent filter.

Single-select vs. Multi-select

Single-select closes the menu and shows the chosen value as text. Multi-select keeps the menu open for further picks and shows each selection as a removable chip in the field — turn it on only when more than one value is a genuinely valid choice.

Open state

Open reveals the options menu directly beneath the field, with the same elevation as any other floating surface. The chevron flips upward and the border switches to the focus ring — never hide the menu without also flipping the chevron back down.

Error & Disabled state

Error pairs a red border and icon with a required supporting-text explanation — never rely on color alone. Disabled means the field cannot be opened right now, not just discouraged from being changed.

Keyboard interactions

Enter or SpaceOpens the menu when the field is focused, or chooses the focused option when the menu is open.
Arrow Down or Arrow UpMoves the highlighted option to the next or previous item in the open menu.
EscapeCloses the menu without changing the selection.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the field, in document order; also closes the menu if it was open.

Code

<Dropdown
  label="Label"
  placeholder="Select an option"
  options={options}
  value={value}
  onChange={setValue}
/>

<Dropdown label="Label" type="multi-select" options={options} value={values} onChange={setValues} />

Date Picker

A form field that reveals a calendar panel on demand for picking a single date, instead of typing or scrolling through a plain text input.

Label
dd/mm/yyyy
Supporting text
December 2026
SMTWTFS

Anatomy

12345
Label
dd/mm/yyyy
Supporting text
December 2026
SMTWTFS
12345678910111213141516171819202122232425262728293031
  1. 1Label — describes the field, recolors to Danger on Error
  2. 2Field — the closed control: optional leading icon, dd/mm/yyyy value or placeholder text, and a trailing calendar icon
  3. 3Calendar panel — Month/Year header with Previous/Next month navigation, a Sun–Sat weekday row, and a grid of day cells
  4. 4Day cell — Default, Hover, or Selected, fully round at 32×32
  5. 5Supporting text — helper copy, or the required explanation under an Error

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Small

Same 3-size scale as Dropdown and Text Input — Small suits dense forms, Medium most forms, Large a single high-emphasis field.

stateEnabled / Hover / Open / Filled / Error / Disableddefault: Enabled

Identical shape to Dropdown’s own State axis: Open reveals the calendar panel, Filled shows a chosen date in place of the placeholder, Error pairs a red border with required supporting text, Disabled means the field can’t be opened.

show leading icontrue / falsedefault: false

Off by default, same as Dropdown — Figma’s own field variants leave a "search" icon wired to this slot (a leftover from the file being cloned from Dropdown), left faithful rather than swapped for something more date-specific since nothing in Figma suggests it should be.

States

Behaviors

  • Open reveals the calendar panel directly beneath the field, at the same elevation as any other floating surface — the border switches to the focus ring, matching Dropdown’s own Open treatment.
  • Selecting a day closes the panel and writes that date into the field as its value text, replacing the placeholder.
  • Previous/Next month navigation re-renders the weekday-aligned day grid for the new month — real calendar math (leap years, days-in-month, day-of-week offset included), not a static lookup, since Figma’s own sample grid is a fixed "December 2026" snapshot rather than a data source.
  • Error pairs a red border with a required supporting-text explanation — never rely on color alone. Disabled means the field cannot be opened right now.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Always show the selected date in the field once chosen
  • Default to the current month when no date is selected
  • Pair error states with a specific, actionable message
Don’t
  • Don’t rely on the placeholder as the only label
  • Don’t hide month navigation controls
  • Don’t use color alone to mark today or the selected day

Usage guidelines

Manual typing vs. calendar-only

Allow typing for known dates; require the calendar for unfamiliar ranges or when format errors are common.

Disabled dates

Grey out and disable dates outside the valid range — don’t just block selection silently.

Error placement

Show inline helper text below the field, paired with an icon — never rely on border color alone.

Label vs. placeholder

Never rely on the placeholder as the only label; keep the label visible above the field at all times.

Today vs. selected

Distinguish "today" (outline) from the selected date (filled) so users can locate both at a glance. Note: Figma’s real Calendar Cell component only ships Default/Hover/Selected states — there is no separate "today" outline variant modeled yet, so this guidance is aspirational relative to the current file; not fabricated here as a 4th cell state.

Keyboard interactions

Enter or SpaceOpens the calendar panel when the field is focused, or chooses the focused day when the panel is open.
Arrow Left or Arrow Right or Arrow Up or Arrow DownMoves focus one day at a time within the open calendar grid.
EscapeCloses the calendar panel without changing the selected date.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus to or away from the field, in document order; also closes the panel if it was open.

Code

<DatePicker
  label="Label"
  value={date}
  onChange={setDate}
/>
