COMPONENTS

Header

The persistent, full-width bar anchoring a product: logo, primary navigation, and utility actions like search, notifications, and account, across desktop, tablet, and mobile.

Project name
DashboardProjectsReportsAnalyticsTeamBilling
Search
Sales reportMarketing reportUsage analytics
NotificationsClear all

Design review requested

10 min ago

Sarah commented on Header

1 hour ago
Alex Kimalex.kim@deloitte.com
ProfilePreferencesSign out
DashboardProjectsReports

Anatomy

123456
DashboardProjects
  1. 1Logo — links back to the product’s homepage on every breakpoint
  2. 2Primary nav item — up to 6 top-level destinations; the current one is underlined
  3. 3Search — an icon-only trigger or a full field, never both at once
  4. 4Notifications — a bell with an unread-count badge, opening an anchored panel
  5. 5Account trigger — avatar, name, and chevron, opening an anchored account menu
  6. 6App switcher — jumps between related products

Options

breakpointDesktop / Tablet / Mobiledefault: Desktop

Use Desktop for screens 1024px and above, with full nav, search field, and all utility icons visible. Tablet condenses nav into fewer visible items. Mobile collapses everything into a hamburger menu, keeping only the logo and menu trigger visible.

search styleIcon / Fielddefault: Icon

Use Icon-only search when horizontal space is limited or search is a secondary action. Use the full Field variant when search is a primary, frequently-used action on the page.

nav items3 / 4 / 5 / 6default: 3

Defaults to 3 visible items. Up to 3 more can be revealed via the “Show Nav Item 4/5/6” properties, for a maximum of 6 — based on cross-system research showing 2–7 items as the common range for top-level header navigation. If a page genuinely needs more, move navigation to a sidebar instead of exceeding 6.

show cta buttonyes / nodefault: no

Show the CTA button only when there’s one clear primary action for the page (e.g. “New Project”). Don’t use it for secondary or tertiary actions — those belong in the nav or a menu.

show search / notifications / settings / account / app switcheryes / no (each independent)default: yes

Each utility icon is its own boolean property, so a surface that doesn’t need one (e.g. no app switcher for a single-product experience) can turn it off without affecting the others.

States

Behaviors

  • Notifications and Account each open as an overlay panel anchored to their trigger icon, not as a separate page. Both are closed by default, and only one may be open at a time — opening one closes the other.
  • A nav item with children (e.g. Reports) opens a small submenu panel of its own on click, without navigating away from the current page.
  • Below the Tablet breakpoint, the primary nav collapses entirely into a hamburger trigger; opening it reveals the same nav items — plus the utility icons that no longer fit — in a full-width dropdown panel instead of a horizontal row.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Keep the same nav items visible across breakpoints — collapse into a menu on mobile rather than hiding items silently
  • Use the CTA button sparingly, for one primary action only
  • Pin the account menu and notifications to the same position across all screen sizes
Don’t
  • Don’t stack more than one row of navigation — collapse into a dropdown instead
  • Don’t show both the search icon and search field at once; pick one per breakpoint
  • Don’t remove the logo’s link back to the homepage on any breakpoint

Usage guidelines

Breakpoint

Use Desktop for screens 1024px and above, with full nav, search field, and all utility icons visible. Tablet condenses nav into fewer visible items. Mobile collapses everything into a hamburger menu, keeping only the logo and menu trigger visible.

Nav Items

Defaults to 3 visible items. Up to 3 more can be revealed via the “Show Nav Item 4/5/6” properties, for a maximum of 6 — based on cross-system research showing 2–7 items as the common range for top-level header navigation. If a page genuinely needs more, move navigation to a sidebar instead of exceeding 6.

Search Style

Use Icon-only search when horizontal space is limited or search is a secondary action. Use the full Field variant when search is a primary, frequently-used action on the page.

CTA Button

Show the CTA button only when there’s one clear primary action for the page (e.g. “New Project”). Don’t use it for secondary or tertiary actions — those belong in the nav or a menu.

Notifications & Account menus

These open as overlays anchored to their trigger icon, not as separate pages. Keep both closed by default; only one should be open at a time.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus through the logo, each visible nav item, and the utility icons, in document order.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused trigger — opens a nav item’s submenu, the notifications panel, the account menu, or the mobile hamburger menu.
EscapeCloses whichever overlay (submenu, notifications, account menu, or mobile menu) is currently open, returning focus to its trigger.

Code

<Header breakpoint="desktop" searchStyle="icon" showCtaButton={false}>
  <NavItem current>Dashboard</NavItem>
  <NavItem>Projects</NavItem>
  <NavItem submenu={['Sales report', 'Marketing report', 'Usage analytics']}>Reports</NavItem>
</Header>

List

A vertical collection of rows — an avatar, primary and supporting text, and an optional leading checkbox or trailing content — for scanning or selecting from a set of items.

ABAlbertoClerk2
AlbertoClerkVerified
AlbertoClerkWIP
AlbertoClerkApproved
AlbertoClerkCancelled

Anatomy

1234
AlbertoClerk
  1. 1Checkbox — optional leading control, shown only on lists that support selection
  2. 2Avatar — Icon, Initials, or Photo, with an optional status dot
  3. 3Text — a primary label and supporting detail beneath it
  4. 4Trailing content — a chevron for a navigable row, or a Status Badge for a state/count callout

Options

stateDefault / Hover / Focused / Pressed / Selected / Disableddefault: Default

Selected takes a tinted Background/Interactive/Subtle fill to mark the row that’s currently open or active. Focused shows a focus ring during keyboard navigation, independent of Selected. Disabled dims the row and removes interaction.

show checkboxtrue / falsedefault: false

Reserve the checkbox for lists that support selection — leave it off for pure navigation lists, where the row itself is the click target.

show trailingtrue / falsedefault: true

Trailing content is an instance-swap slot — typically a chevron for a navigable row, or a Status Badge for a state/count callout. Turn it off for a row with nothing to show at the end.

States

Behaviors

  • Selected takes a tinted Background/Interactive/Subtle fill to mark the row that’s currently open or active — it persists until another row is selected or navigation changes, unlike Hover which is purely transient.
  • Focused shows a Border/Focus/Default ring during keyboard navigation, moving independently of which row is Selected.
  • Disabled removes pointer and keyboard interaction entirely and dims the avatar and text to Text/Disabled/On Disabled — it’s mutually exclusive with Selected.
  • Rows separate with a hairline Border/Default/Primary bottom border on Default; the Hover, Pressed, and Selected fills read as the separator instead of the hairline.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Reserve the checkbox for lists that support selection; leave it off for pure navigation lists
  • Use the Status Badge for state/count callouts and the chevron for navigable rows — not both at once
  • Swap the avatar between Photo, Icon, and Initials per row depending on what data is actually available
  • Reserve the Selected state for the row currently open or active, not just hovered
Don’t
  • Don’t show a checkbox and a navigation chevron on the same row — that mixes selection with navigation
  • Don’t mark a row Disabled while it’s Selected; treat the two states as mutually exclusive
  • Don’t stretch or recolor the avatar outside its Photo/Icon/Initials variants
  • Don’t drop the divider between rows in a dense list; it’s what separates one recipient from the next

Usage guidelines

Checkbox vs. no checkbox

Show the checkbox only in lists that support selecting rows for a bulk action (approve, delete, export). Leave it off entirely for lists that exist purely for navigation or browsing.

Status Badge vs. Chevron

Use the Status Badge when the row's trailing content is reporting a state or count (Verified, WIP, a notification count). Use the chevron when the row itself is tappable and leads somewhere else — never both.

Avatar: Photo / Icon / Initials

Prefer Photo when a real image is available. Fall back to Initials when you have a name but no photo, and to the generic Icon variant for system accounts or entities that aren't a person at all.

Selected vs. Hover

Selected marks the row that's currently open or active, and persists until something else is chosen. Hover is a transient pointer state only — never use it to indicate what's currently selected.

Disabled state

Disabled communicates a row that exists but can't currently be acted on (e.g. a recipient who's already been removed). Dim the whole row, not just the trailing content, so the non-interactive intent reads at a glance.

Keyboard interactions

Arrow Down or Arrow UpMoves focus to the next or previous row in the list.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused row — opens it, or toggles its checkbox when one is shown.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus into or out of the list as a whole, in document order.

Code

<List>
  <ListItem
    avatar={{ type: 'icon', icon: 'person-outline' }}
    title="Alberto"
    supportingText="Clerk"
    trailing={<Icon name="chevron-forward" />}
  />
  <ListItem showCheckbox avatar={{ type: 'photo', src: alberto.jpg }} title="Alberto" supportingText="Clerk" trailing={<StatusBadge tone="info">Verified</StatusBadge>} />
</List>

Card

A bounded container for a self-contained piece of content — header, body, and optional actions — in one of three real layouts: Slot (a generic content slot), Horizontal (a compact side-by-side row), or Stacked (a fixed media + body layout).

HeadlineSubheader
Label
Content slot
HeadlineSubheader
Label
HeadlineSubheader
Label
Media
TitleSubtitle

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor

Anatomy

12345
HeadlineSubheader
Label
Content
  1. 1Leading icon — an optional avatar/icon in the header, Slot and Stacked only
  2. 2Headline & Subheader — both render in the same primary ink color, differentiated by size and weight rather than color
  3. 3Tertiary actions — a text label paired with a "more" icon for overflow actions
  4. 4Content — a Slot (arbitrary child content) for Slot Card, or a fixed media/body layout for Stacked Card
  5. 5Actions — a Secondary + Primary button pair, Round/Small, anchored to the bottom

Options

typeSlot / Horizontal / Stackeddefault: Slot

These are 3 separate real Figma components, not variants of one component set. Slot Card exposes a generic Card Slot for arbitrary content (348px content area). Horizontal Card is a fixed 480×80 row with a colored leading accent block, for a compact, list-like presentation. Stacked Card is a fixed header + media + body + actions layout with no exposed properties — every part is always shown.

show headline / show subheadertrue / falsedefault: true

Slot Card only — Horizontal and Stacked always show both. Turning off Headline while leaving Subheader on is a real, valid combination in the underlying component.

show leading icontrue / falsedefault: true

Slot Card only — Horizontal Card has no leading icon property (its leading accent block is a fixed star icon, not a swappable avatar), and Stacked Card's leading icon has no exposed toggle.

show trailing icon / show trailing icon texttrue / falsedefault: true

Independent toggles for the tertiary-actions "more" icon and its adjacent text label — available on both Slot and Horizontal Card.

States

Behaviors

  • Slot Card's content area is a real Figma SLOT property — it accepts arbitrary child content (an image, a chart, a form, anything), unlike Stacked Card's Media area, which is a fixed, non-slotted frame in the component.
  • Horizontal Card ships with a ButtonGroup in its source component, but it's hidden by default with no exposed boolean to reveal it — treat the row as header-only unless a future Figma update exposes that toggle.
  • Headline and Subheader always render in the same Text/Default/Primary ink color across all 3 card types — Subheader is set apart by its smaller size and regular weight, not a lighter text color.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Slot Card when content varies (image, chart, custom layout) — its content area is a real slot
  • Use Horizontal Card for a compact, list-like row
  • Keep the Actions row to the real Secondary + Primary pair only
  • Lean on Headline's size and weight for hierarchy, since Headline and Subheader share the same ink color
Don’t
  • Don't pick Stacked Card expecting to hide or swap its parts — none of them are toggleable
  • Don't add a third action button; the source component only ships two
  • Don't use the header's "more" label + icon for a frequent action — that belongs in the Actions row
  • Don't expect Subheader to read as de-emphasized from color alone

Usage guidelines

Choosing a type

Use Slot Card when the card's content varies (an image, a chart, a custom layout) — its content area is a true slot. Use Horizontal Card for a compact, list-like row where a card would otherwise take too much vertical space. Use Stacked Card only when the fixed media + body + two-button layout matches your content exactly, since none of its parts are individually toggleable.

Tertiary actions

Reserve the header's Label + "more" icon for overflow actions that don't deserve a full button — anything a user would do often belongs in the Actions row instead, not tucked into the header.

Actions row

Keep to the real Secondary + Primary pair — Secondary for a lower-emphasis action (e.g. "Dismiss"), Primary for the card's one clear next step (e.g. "View details"). Don't add a third button; the source component only ships two.

Headline vs. Subheader

Since both render in the same ink color, lean on Headline's larger size and Medium weight to carry the visual hierarchy — don't expect color to do that work for you.

Keyboard interactions

Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus through the card's interactive parts — the "more" trigger, then each action button — in document order.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused "more" trigger or action button.

Code

<Card type="slot" headline="Headline" subheader="Subheader">
  <CardSlot>{/* any content */}</CardSlot>
  <CardActions>
    <Button type="secondary" shape="round" size="small">Label</Button>
    <Button type="primary" shape="round" size="small">Label</Button>
  </CardActions>
</Card>

<Card type="horizontal" headline="Headline" subheader="Subheader" label="Label" />

Segmented Control

A single-select group of mutually exclusive options, exactly one always selected.

Anatomy

123
  1. 1Track — the pill-shaped container that holds every segment
  2. 2Segment — one option, Selected or Unselected, each with its own Enabled/Focused/Disabled state
  3. 3Focus ring — appears on the focused segment during keyboard navigation, independent of which one is Selected

Options

sizeSmall / Medium / Largedefault: Small

Small fits dense toolbars and compact panels. Medium is the default for most content areas. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

segments2 / 3 / 4default: 2

Segmented Control supports 2 to 4 segments. For more options, switch to Tabs or a dropdown so the control doesn’t get cramped or hard to scan.

stateEnabled / Focused / Disableddefault: Enabled

A per-segment property in Figma — Focused appears only during keyboard navigation, and Disabled is normally applied to the whole control at once rather than a single segment.

States

Behaviors

  • Exactly one segment is Selected at all times; choosing a new segment deselects the previous one — a segmented control switches between views, it isn’t a multi-select.
  • Focused appears only during keyboard navigation and moves independently of which segment is Selected.
  • A disabled segment can’t be selected via click or keyboard, while the rest of the control stays interactive.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use a segmented control when there are 2–4 mutually exclusive views or filters that should all be visible at once
  • Keep exactly one segment selected so the current view is always clear
  • Match the Size variant to the density of the surrounding layout
Don’t
  • Don’t use a segmented control for more than 4 options — move to Tabs or a dropdown instead
  • Don’t leave zero segments selected, or allow more than one selected at a time
  • Don’t use it for independent on/off choices — use Checkbox or Toggle Switch for that

Usage guidelines

Number of segments

Segmented Control supports 2 to 4 segments. For more options, switch to Tabs or a dropdown so the control doesn’t get cramped or hard to scan.

Size scale

Small fits dense toolbars and compact panels. Medium is the default for most content areas. Large suits touch-first or high-emphasis contexts.

Selected state

Exactly one segment is Selected at all times — segmented controls switch between views, they are not for independent multi-select choices.

Focused state

Focused only appears during keyboard navigation and moves independently of which segment is currently Selected.

Disabled state

Disable an individual segment only when that view or filter is genuinely unavailable right now, while keeping the rest of the control interactive.

Keyboard interactions

Arrow Left or Arrow RightMoves focus to the previous or next segment.
Enter or SpaceSelects the focused segment.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus into or out of the control as a whole, in document order.

Code

<SegmentedControl size="medium" value={view} onChange={setView}>
  <Segment value="list">List</Segment>
  <Segment value="board">Board</Segment>
  <Segment value="calendar">Calendar</Segment>
</SegmentedControl>

Slider

A draggable control for selecting a single value or a range along a continuous horizontal or vertical scale.

Label4520 – 70
Supporting text

Anatomy

12345
Label45
Supporting text
  1. 1Label row — the field label and current value (or range), each optional
  2. 2Track — the full-length background bar
  3. 3Active track — fills from the start (or between two thumbs, for Range) to show the current value
  4. 4Thumb — one draggable handle for Single, two for Range
  5. 5Supporting text — optional helper copy below the track

Options

typeSingle / Rangedefault: Single

Use Single to set one value on a scale. Use Range when users need to define both a minimum and maximum, such as a price band.

sizeSmall / Mediumdefault: Medium

Medium is the default track and handle size for most content. Small suits dense panels or secondary controls where the slider isn’t the primary interaction.

orientationHorizontal / Verticaldefault: Horizontal

Horizontal fits most layouts and reads left-to-right as the value increases. Vertical suits compact side panels or bottom-to-top scales. Range doesn’t ship a Vertical variant in Figma — pair Range with Horizontal only.

show label / show supporting texttrue / false (each independent)default: true

Turn both off when the slider sits in an already-labeled context — for example, next to its own field label in a form — to avoid duplicate labeling.

States

Behaviors

  • Hover shows a soft halo behind the thumb; Focused shows a ring instead — the two never appear together.
  • Active reflects an in-progress drag, thickening the thumb’s ring — it’s a transient gesture state, not a static “selected” indicator.
  • Disabled dims the track, active track, and thumb together and removes drag interaction entirely.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use Range when users need to set both a minimum and maximum, and Single when there’s only one value to choose
  • Show the label and supporting text whenever the numeric value or its meaning isn’t obvious on its own
  • Choose Horizontal or Vertical orientation to match the layout it lives in
Don’t
  • Don’t use a slider for precise numeric entry — pair it with an input field when exact values matter
  • Don’t hide the current value if its position on the track isn’t visually obvious
  • Don’t mix Horizontal and Vertical sliders for the same kind of control within one flow

Usage guidelines

Single vs. Range

Use Single to set one value on a scale. Use Range when users need to define both a minimum and maximum, such as a price band.

Orientation

Horizontal fits most layouts and reads left-to-right as the value increases. Vertical suits compact side panels or bottom-to-top scales.

Size scale

Medium is the default track and handle size for most content. Small suits dense panels or secondary controls where the slider isn’t the primary interaction.

Label & supporting text

Show the label and supporting text whenever the value’s meaning or unit isn’t obvious on its own, such as currency, percentage, or duration.

Interaction states

Hover and Focused appear before a drag begins, Active reflects an in-progress drag, and Disabled is used only when the setting can’t currently be changed.

Keyboard interactions

Arrow Left or Arrow RightDecreases or increases the focused thumb’s value by one step (Arrow Up / Arrow Down for a Vertical slider).
Home or EndJumps the focused thumb to its minimum or maximum value.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves focus between the two thumbs on a Range slider, or into and out of the control on Single.

Code

<Slider label="Volume" value={45} onChange={setValue} />

<Slider type="range" label="Price" value={[20, 80]} onChange={setRange} supportingText="USD" />

Accordion

A vertical stack of collapsible header+body rows for progressively disclosing content — Accordion Item is the stateless single row; Accordion Pattern is the sibling-aware list that decides which one(s) stay open.

Body copy for this accordion item goes here. It can wrap across multiple lines as needed.

Body copy for this accordion item goes here. It can wrap across multiple lines as needed.

Body copy for this accordion item goes here. It can wrap across multiple lines as needed.

Body copy for this accordion item goes here. It can wrap across multiple lines as needed.

Anatomy

12345
Accordion item titleSupporting description text

Body copy for this accordion item goes here. It can wrap across multiple lines as needed.

  1. 1Leading icon — optional, shown only when Show Leading Icon is on
  2. 2Text column — a Title, plus an optional Description shown only when Show Description is on
  3. 3Chevron — rotates 180° open/closed in code; the two directions baked into Figma preview both ends of that rotation, not two separate icon assets
  4. 4Body — the row’s expanded content, revealed only when Expanded
  5. 5Divider — Lines style only, the hairline separating one stacked item from the next (Shapes style wraps each item in its own bordered card instead)

Options

styleLines / Shapesdefault: Lines

Lines is a flush, divider-separated list — the style Accordion Pattern’s own real example stacks. Shapes wraps each item in its own 8px-radius bordered card.

sizeSmall / Mediumdefault: Small

Small uses 12px header padding; Medium steps up to 16px. Both share the same Body/Medium-emphasized title and Body/Small description type.

stateDefault / Hover / Focused / Pressed / Disableddefault: Default

Focused shows a 2px ring on the header for keyboard navigation. Pressed takes a Background/Default/Secondary Hover fill. Disabled removes interaction only — verified directly against Figma, it ships no separate dimmed visual.

expandedCollapsed / Expandeddefault: Collapsed

Reveals the Body row and rotates the chevron 180° — click the header itself for the same effect.

show leading icontrue / falsedefault: false

Off by default in Figma — turn on only when an icon adds real meaning per item.

show descriptiontrue / falsedefault: false

A second line under the Title, independent of Expanded — a short qualifier that should stay visible even while collapsed.

States

Behaviors

  • In code, use one chevron icon and rotate it 180° on toggle — the Collapsed/Expanded chevron variants baked into Figma preview both ends of that rotation, not two separate icon assets.
  • Focused shows a 2px ring on the header itself, bound to the same primitive Orbit’s other focus rings use (Brand Teal/700) — it never appears together with Hover.
  • Disabled removes pointer and keyboard interaction but carries no distinct dimmed fill in Figma — every Disabled variant’s fill and stroke are identical to Default, verified via direct node reads rather than the variant-summary tool.
  • Accordion Pattern is a separate component that owns which sibling(s) stay open — Accordion Item itself only knows its own open/closed look. Single-expand (one item open at a time) is the file’s own recommended default; Multi-expand allows several open at once.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Keep header titles short and scannable, ideally one line
  • Show a visible focus ring so keyboard users can track their place
  • Make the entire header row the click target, not just the icon
  • Default to single-expand (one section open at a time) unless comparing content across sections is a real need
Don’t
  • Don’t nest accordions more than one level deep
  • Don’t hide required or critical content inside a collapsed panel
  • Don’t disable an item without explaining why elsewhere on the page
  • Don’t put interactive elements (buttons, links) inside the header — it’s already a button, so nesting one breaks accessibility

Usage guidelines

Accordion Item vs. Accordion Pattern

Accordion Item is a stateless, presentational row — it only knows its own open/closed look. Accordion Pattern owns what no single item can: which sibling(s) are open, and how opening one affects the others — built by stacking Accordion Item instances together. The Behavior variant only documents that split; enforcing single- vs. multi-expand still has to be written in code.

Single-expand vs. multi-expand

Allow only one item open at a time when sections are mutually exclusive steps; allow several open at once when users need to compare content across sections.

Focused / Hover

Hover is a light background tint that previews interactivity on pointer devices. Focus is a visible teal ring reserved for keyboard navigation — never remove it for the sake of visual polish.

Disabled state

Use sparingly, only when a section is genuinely unavailable right now (e.g. locked behind a prior step). Explain why elsewhere on the page rather than leaving users guessing.

Nesting accordions

Avoid nesting one accordion inside another. If content feels like it needs two levels, it usually means the information architecture should be flattened or split into separate pages instead.

Icon rotates, it does not swap

In code, use one chevron icon and rotate it 180° on toggle (Cloudscape, Carbon, and Fluent all do this). The two chevron states baked into this Figma component exist to preview both ends of that rotation, not to imply two separate icon assets.

Keyboard navigation between headers

Support Enter/Space to toggle the focused header. For full parity with Fluent’s model, also support Arrow Up/Down to move focus between headers, and Home/End to jump to the first/last header.

Icon position

Right-aligned is Orbit’s default. Left-aligned is a supported alternative — it’s the default convention in Salesforce Lightning and on macOS — but keep it consistent within a single product surface.

Keyboard interactions

Enter or SpaceToggles the focused header open or closed.
Arrow Down or Arrow UpMoves focus to the next or previous header, for full parity with Fluent’s model.
Home or EndJumps focus to the first or last header in the group.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus into or out of the group as a whole, in document order.

Code

<Accordion behavior="single-expand">
  <AccordionItem title="What is Orbit Design System?">
    Orbit is our shared library of tokens, components, and patterns.
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem title="How do I request a new component?" />
</Accordion>

Anatomy

1234
NameActions
EcoGoodshello@ecogoods.com
  1. 1Checkbox column — optional leading control on both the header and every row, for bulk selection
  2. 2Header cell — a column label with an optional sort icon, Default or Hover
  3. 3Cell — swaps between Text, Avatar + Text, Tag, Progress, Checkbox, or Actions depending on the kind of data in that column
  4. 4Row — Enabled, Hover, Selected, or Disabled, separated from the next row by a hairline bottom border

Options

show checkbox columntrue / falsedefault: true

Include it only when the table supports bulk actions (delete, export, assign) — the header row’s own checkbox collapses along with it.

show sort icontrue / falsedefault: true

2026-09-29 re-sync: TableHeaderCell has only two real states, Default and Hover, but each cell genuinely carries TWO real icons side by side — a "sort" glyph (double-headed up/down arrows) and a "chevron" (Direction=down) — neither is a direction indicator on its own. Figma’s own "Show Icon" boolean property exists but isn’t bound to either icon’s visibility in the file (verified directly); this toggle is a best-effort stand-in that shows/hides both together. Show which column and direction is actually active elsewhere (e.g. a bold label). No filter icon exists on this component in Figma — verified directly, not added here.

row stateEnabled / Hover / Selected / Disableddefault: Enabled

Selected pairs with the header checkbox to confirm a checked row. Disabled communicates a row that can’t currently be acted on — verified directly against Figma, it dims nothing at all; only its checkbox and row actions actually go inert.

States

Behaviors

  • The header row’s own Background/Default/Secondary fill separates it from the body without needing a border.
  • A row’s Enabled and Disabled states share the exact same fill, stroke, and text color in Figma — a real, verified exception to the usual “dim it” convention; only its checkbox and row actions actually stop responding.
  • Selected takes a tinted Background/Interactive/Subtle fill, the same token List uses for its own Selected row.
  • Every row separates from the next with a hairline Border/Default/Primary bottom border only — Figma binds no border to the other three sides.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Show the checkbox column only when rows support bulk actions (delete, export, assign)
  • Show the header sort icon only on columns that are genuinely sortable
  • Use the Progress cell for a measurable percentage, and the Tag cell for a qualitative status
Don’t
  • Don’t rely on the sort icon alone to show which direction a column is currently sorted — pair it with a bold header or active-state styling
  • Don’t disable a row without also disabling its checkbox and row actions
  • Don’t mix Progress and Tag cells for the same kind of data across rows

Usage guidelines

Checkbox column

Include it when the table supports bulk actions. Omit it for read-only or single-action lists to reduce visual noise — the header row’s checkbox column collapses along with it.

Sort icon

TableHeaderCell has only two states, Default and Hover — the up/down sort icon is a single Show Icon toggle, not a direction indicator. Turn it on for sortable columns and off for the rest; show which column and direction is active elsewhere (e.g. a bold label).

Row states

Hover previews interactivity, Selected confirms a checked row (pairs with the header checkbox), and Disabled communicates a row that can’t currently be acted on — dim it rather than removing it.

Progress vs. Priority

Use the Progress cell for a quantifiable percentage. Use the Tag cell for a qualitative status so the two data types are never visually confused.

Identity cell

Use the avatar + text cell to identify the row’s primary entity by name and a recognizable image. Fall back to a plain text cell when there’s no meaningful image to show.

Keyboard interactions

Arrow Down or Arrow UpMoves focus to the next or previous row.
SpaceToggles the focused row’s checkbox, when the checkbox column is shown.
EnterActivates the focused row’s primary action, or a focused Actions-cell icon button.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus between interactive cells — checkboxes, sortable header cells, and action icon buttons — in document order.

Code

<Table>
  <TableHeader showCheckbox>
    <TableHeaderCell showIcon>Name</TableHeaderCell>
    <TableHeaderCell showIcon>Progress</TableHeaderCell>
    <TableHeaderCell>Priority</TableHeaderCell>
  </TableHeader>
  <TableRow state="enabled">
    <TableCell type="avatar-text" title="EcoGoods" subtitle="hello@ecogoods.com" />
    <TableCell type="progress" value={82} />
    <TableCell type="tag" label="High" />
  </TableRow>
</Table>

Anatomy

123456
Orbit
Search
Dashboard
Item label
Account
  1. 1Logo — the Deloitte wordmark plus an optional Project Name, shown only in Expanded; Collapsed shows the compact mark alone
  2. 2Search — a real Search field instance in the layer tree, hidden by default in Figma with no exposed toggle to reveal it
  3. 3Tree Item — a nav row with a label and an optional trailing chevron for destinations that have children; the leading icon only appears on a top-level destination, never on a nested one, however deep; up to two extra indent levels are added via a branch Divider
  4. 4Icon Tile — the icon-only equivalent of a Tree Item, shown in Collapsed; a destination with children opens a flyout menu on click instead of expanding inline
  5. 5Toggle — the chevron button that switches the whole rail between Expanded and Collapsed
  6. 6Divider — separates the primary destinations from a secondary Account / Help / Settings group

Options

layoutExpanded / Collapseddefault: Expanded

Expanded is 306px wide with full labels and hierarchy. Collapsed is 68px, icon-only — content and hierarchy stay identical, only the presentation changes.

state (per row)Default / Hover / Focused / Pressed / Selected / Disableddefault: Default

A per-row property in Figma, shown here on the Dashboard row — Focused adds a 2px focus ring implemented as a non-layout-shifting outline, since Figma’s own Focused variant grows the row 44→48px, which this site deliberately avoids reproducing. Selected is also driven directly by clicking any real row, mutually exclusive across the whole rail.

leading icontrue / falsedefault: true

A real per-row Tree Item boolean, shown here on the Dashboard row. This demo only turns it on for top-level destinations — a nested row never shows one, regardless of how deep — so a person scanning the rail can tell a main page from a submenu item at a glance.

trailing icontrue / falsedefault: false

A second, independent icon slot before the branch chevron, off by default in Figma’s own componentPropertyDefinitions — distinct from the chevron itself, which is a separate "Expand/Collapse" property.

show searchtrue / falsedefault: false

The Search field exists in Figma’s own layer tree but ships hidden with no exposed boolean — this toggle is this site’s own addition so the field can still be previewed.

show project nametrue / falsedefault: true

Pairs a divider and a "Project name" label next to the logo, matching Figma’s real default (visible) in the Expanded layout.

States

Behaviors

  • Selected persists on whichever destination matches the current screen and doesn’t move on hover — clicking any Tree Item or Icon Tile moves it there instead, deselecting the previous one.
  • A branch (trailing chevron) reveals its own children when clicked — a real, working expand/collapse, not just a static look; a leaf is terminal and never carries a chevron — verified per-row directly against the real Tree Item instances. The chevron itself also recolors on expand (Icon/Default/Primary) vs. collapse (Icon/Default/Tertiary), a real, distinct token pair, not the same color reused.
  • Disabled dims only the label and icon color (Text/Disabled/On Disabled, Icon/Disabled/Default) — the row’s own background fill is unchanged, the same faithful-but-counter-intuitive pattern already verified on List and Table.
  • In Collapsed, clicking an Icon Tile whose destination has children opens a flyout menu instead of expanding the rail inline; clicking a flyout item that itself has children cascades a second flyout beside the first — this two-level cascade is real Figma content (its own two draft flyout frames on the Credit Cards tile turned out to be a level-1/level-2 pair, not two competing designs, once cross-checked with the user).
  • The collapse Toggle and the Layout property stay in sync in both directions, the same dual-binding already used by Segmented Control and Table.

Do’s & Don’ts

Do
  • Use the collapsed rail when horizontal space is tight, and reserve the expanded state for when labels and hierarchy need to stay visible
  • Keep the current page visually distinct with the Selected state so orientation is obvious at a glance
  • Group related destinations under a Section Header or a branch Tree Item instead of listing every page flat
Don’t
  • Don’t nest more than one level deep — if a group’s children need children of their own, that content belongs on its own page, not deeper in the sidebar
  • Don’t rely on the icon alone to convey a destination when collapsed — pair it with the hover flyout so the label is never fully lost
  • Don’t mix Section Header groups and ungrouped top-level items inconsistently — pick one organizing pattern per sidebar

Usage guidelines

Expanded vs. Collapsed

Use Expanded by default wherever width allows; switch to Collapsed to reclaim space on narrower viewports or when the user manually toggles it. Content and hierarchy stay identical — only the presentation changes.

Section Header vs. flat Tree Item

Use a Section Header when items belong to a named group, like "My organization" or "Shared". Use a flat top-level Tree Item when a destination stands on its own, like Dashboard or Settings.

Branch vs. Leaf

A branch (folder icon, chevron) is for a destination that reveals its own children. A leaf is a terminal destination with no further nesting — don’t give a leaf a chevron.

Selected state

Apply Selected to exactly one Tree Item at a time: whichever destination matches the current page, so the sidebar always shows the user where they are.

Badges vs. chevrons

Use a badge to surface a count that needs attention, like pending items. Use a chevron only to indicate expand/collapse or that the row navigates elsewhere. Never combine both on the same row.

Keyboard interactions

Arrow Down or Arrow UpMoves keyboard focus between destinations in the rail, in visual order.
Enter or SpaceActivates the focused destination, opens a Collapsed flyout, or toggles Expanded/Collapsed when the Toggle button is focused.
Tab or Shift+TabMoves keyboard focus into or out of the rail as a whole, in document order.

Code

<Sidebar layout="expanded" currentItem="dashboard">
  <SidebarSearch />
  <TreeItem icon="home" label="Dashboard" current />
  <TreeItem icon="group" label="Customers" expandable>
    <TreeItem label="Refunds" level={2} />
    <TreeItem label="Declines" level={2} />
  </TreeItem>
  <SidebarDivider />
  <TreeItem icon="person-outline" label="Account" />
</Sidebar>
